plan.topic: Plague and marmots: why marmots, not rats, are a key plague reservoir in Siberia, Mongolia and China
plan.angle: Title: 'Plague and Marmots: Why Marmots Matter for Plague in Mongolia and Siberia #shorts'. In natural plague foci in Mongolia and southern Siberia, marmots and their fleas, along with other wild rodents, help keep Yersinia pestis circulating. Hunting, skinning or eating infected marmots has been linked to human bubonic cases. Mongolia's NCZD reported marmot-linked cases in Aug 2026 (as reported by the Moscow Times; use their exact suspected/confirmed wording). Treat eating marmot respectfully as a cultural tradition. Prevention: don't handle sick or dead wild animals, and wear gloves if you're skinning animals (CDC). Add the dated Irkutsk status hedge with no marmot link. Close with the urgent-contact line and 'If you're worried, talk to a health professional.'

plan.why: National Geographic published on this Oct 9 and nobody on YouTube links it to the news yet. It gives evergreen Plague 101 a timely hook with low competition. | fact-check: Good evergreen Plague 101 topic, but three fixes. (1) 'Marmots, not rats' overstates it. Natural plague foci in this region also involve ground squirrels, gerbils and pikas, and rats are still reservoirs elsewhere. (2) The Mongolia Aug 2026 reports aren't consistent. A Moscow Times item (themoscowtimes.com/2026/08/04) cites Mongolia's NCZD on two 'suspected' cases linked to marmot meat but also says lab tests confirmed them, and other outlets report a death in Khovd on Aug 11. Open the Moscow Times article, check its date and content, and copy its exact status wording, credited to Mongolia's NCZD as reported by the Moscow Times. (3) I couldn't verify the claim that Rospotrebnadzor has warned against marmot hunting. Source it or drop it. Keep the respectful cultural context, use no horror imagery, and make no link to Irkutsk.

package.title: Plague in Mongolia: Why Marmots Are a Key Host #shorts
package.description:
Plague bacteria live in wild small mammals and their fleas (WHO). In Mongolia, a key host is the marmot (Emerging Microbes & Infections, 2020). In 2019, two people in western Mongolia died of lab-confirmed plague after eating raw marmot organs.

This content is for educational purposes only and is not medical advice. Always talk to a qualified healthcare professional about your own situation. Fever, chills, a swollen painful lymph node, stomach pain, cough, shortness of breath or chest pain after handling or eating a wild animal? Contact a doctor or local health authority urgently. If you're worried, talk to a health professional.

Sources:
Two fatal cases of plague after consumption of raw marmot organs (Emerging Microbes & Infections, 2020): https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7473306/
Plague (fact sheet) (WHO, 2026): https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/plague
How Plague Spreads (CDC, 2024): https://www.cdc.gov/plague/causes/index.html
Preventing Plague (CDC, 2025): https://www.cdc.gov/plague/prevention/index.html

script.cta: Plague is rare, and antibiotics work best when started early. If you're worried, talk to a health professional.

factcheck.summary: I checked every factual claim against its cited source. They all hold up. Kehrmann et al. (Emerging Microbes & Infections, 2020) supports each detail in s4. The cases were in 2019, in Bayan-Ölgii province in western Mongolia, and two people died: a 38-year-old man and his 37-year-old wife. Y. pestis was confirmed by culture, PCR and phage lysis. They had eaten raw marmot kidney, stomach and gallbladder. The paper says "hunting marmots has been prohibited by the Mongolian government since 2014", calls marmot meat "a delicacy" and says marmots "are the main reservoir of Y. pestis in Mongolia". The CDC pages also match. Plague spreads by flea bites and by handling infected tissue, and CDC gives the example of skinning an animal without gloves (reviewed May 15, 2024). CDC's glove and dead-animal advice is quoted almost word for word (reviewed Mar 5, 2025). The symptom list covers bubonic, septicemic and pneumonic plague, and all 4 of CDC's pneumonic signs are present (reviewed May 15, 2024). The "rare" and "cured with antibiotics… given promptly" lines also match CDC (reviewed Aug 24, 2026). The WHO fact sheet (updated Sep 29, 2026) supports the treatment line and says the bacteria live in small mammals and their fleas. The wording is hedged correctly, the cultural beat is respectful and doesn't blame anyone, the urgent-contact line and the safety line are both there, and there's no fear-bait. The issues below are all minor wording fixes. This is an evergreen Plague 101 piece with no Irkutsk status claims, so it doesn't need a status line.

issues.claim: Fever after animal contact? Contact a doctor urgently
issues.problem: The on-screen text drops 'or local health authority', which the craft rules require us to keep. It also shrinks the full symptom list in the narration down to 'fever'.

issues.claim: Plague is rare, and treatable when caught early.
issues.problem: This is slightly narrower than s6 ('treatable, especially when started early') and than CDC ('can be cured with antibiotics, but these must be given promptly'). It could be read as saying plague is only treatable when caught early. Use the same wording in every scene.
issues.fix: Narration and cta: "Plague is rare, and antibiotics work best when started early. If you're worried, talk to a health professional." On-screen: "Rare. Treat early."

issues.claim: Yersinia pestis... survives in wild rodents and their fleas.
issues.problem: WHO's wording is 'small mammals and their fleas'. 'Rodents' is close enough for marmots, but quoting the source exactly is safer.
issues.fix: Yersinia pestis, the plague bacterium, lives in wild small mammals, like rodents, and their fleas. In Mongolia, a key host is the marmot.

issues.problem: The script says marmot hunting has been banned since 2014. A hunter on screen could look like we endorse illegal hunting.

audio.soundNotes: Music sits in the right window under speech (-13.5dB) but was a touch hot in pauses (-12.5 vs ~-14 target), so pulled the whole bed down ~1.4dB (0.85x); pause and reveal moments (t52.3, t68.8, t73.4) already measured -8 to -12dB and were left untouched since they're on target. The 4.2–4.8s 'Yersinia pestis' zoom had 13 overlapping bubble/swoosh layers in under a second — thinned to one whoosh + closing blip. Several other transitions doubled up redundant swoosh/whoosh/whip pairs (11.6s, 14.4s, 29.4s, 38.2s, 47.3s, 60.3s, 63.9s, 68.8s) — kept one of each pair and dropped the duplicate. Reduced a cluster of 5 effects crammed into 43.7–44.3s ('Local health department') to 4 by cutting one swoosh and taming two cues that read 12–13dB under voice (too loud for in-speech SFX) down toward the -17dB range. Thinned the 'Rare. Treat early.' one-liner to just a swell, a hit and one pop, consistent with keeping SFX sparse on serious/dramatic lines. Added five short bespoke SFX for key story beats (marmot intro, banned stamp, pill-bottle antibiotics cue, calm medical alert pulse for urgent care, soft heartbeat under the closing reassurance) at low, speech-safe gains so they add flavor without competing with narration.

issues.claim: People can get infected from flea bites, or by handling or skinning an infected animal without gloves (CDC).
issues.problem: The script says 'handling an infected animal, like skinning it without gloves'. The captions make 'without gloves' apply to all handling, which suggests risk exists only without gloves. That is narrower than the script and the CDC wording.
issues.fix: Instagram: "People can get infected from flea bites, or by handling an infected animal, like skinning it without gloves (CDC)." Facebook: "...and people can get infected from flea bites or by handling an infected animal, like skinning it without gloves (CDC)."

issues.claim: Think marmots: a key host there, alongside fleas.
issues.problem: Fleas are vectors, not hosts. The script says Y. pestis lives in wild small mammals and their fleas. 'Alongside fleas' makes fleas a co-host.
issues.fix: Plague in Mongolia? Think marmots. Plague bacteria live in wild small mammals and their fleas, and in Mongolia a key host is the marmot.

issues.claim: Had you heard marmots carry plague risk, or did you think it was all about rats? Tell us below.
